newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn wants action as first German-born cow has BSE.
newsitem.headline: Bonn wants action as first German-born cow has BSE.

text.p: Germany on Tuesday confirmed the first case of a cow born in the country to die of mad cow disease and called on the European Union to act soon to prevent similar cases.

The Agriculture Ministry confirmed that tests on the brain of the Galloway cow had shown signs of bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE). The cow was born in Germany in 1992, the calf of a cow imported from Britain.
Germany has had four previous cases of BSE but all in cattle imported from Britain, where the disease is most widespread with 165,000 cases in the past 10 years.
The possibility that the cow was infected by contaminated feed had been ruled out, the ministry said, leaving only the possibility that it had been infected by its mother.
The European Union already maintains a wide-ranging ban on almost all exports of British beef products and cattle.

Health Minister Horst Seehofer said in a statement the latest case meant the EU should as quickly as possible agree unified measures to tackle the possibility of transmission from British cows in other countries to their calves.
An EU veterinary committee is due to report in March on whether maternal transmission from cow to calf is possible and how it occurs.

The Agriculture Ministry said initial protective measures had been taken in Germany last year against the possibility of mother-to-calf transmission, when the offspring of cows from British farms with cases of BSE were put under observation.
It said there was a ban on the slaughter of such cows and meat from these animals could not get into the food chain.
The Health Ministry reiterated this reassurance but said it must now review whether further measures were necessary to ensure consumer safety.

Since the mad cow crisis erupted in March 1996 when Britain established a likely link between BSE and its human equivalent, Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease, Germany has taken the toughest stance on protecting public health.

The German Agriculture and Health Ministries said they had invited top officials, vets and scientists to a meeting in Bonn on Wednesday to look at the details of the case and decide what should be done with British as well as Swiss cows in Germany.
Switzerland has the most cows infected with BSE after Britain.

The Agriculture Ministry said that in April 1996 there were 3,400 cows imported from Britain in the country. It estimated that with their offspring there were now around 10,000 cows of British origin in Germany.
